We introduce a concept for the p-divisibility transposition of the Fourier coefficients 
of Siegel modular forms. This concept complements the Wilton result on p-divisibility for the Ramanujan $\tau$-function.

In 2009, B. Colbois and O. Kappeler introduced Rigid Fibrations as a macroscopically collapsed fiber bundles with a positive Laplacian spectrum. They had a conjecture about their associated cohomology groups, which remains unproven. This paper confirms part of their hypothesis by showing that every Rigid Fibration has a subalgebra of its smooth functions that maps to a finite-dimensional quotient with zero cohomology groups in degrees greater than one.

The phenomenon of the Pauli Exclusion Principle in Helium-3 and Helium-4 is explored through a statistical mechanical framework. Research demonstrates the absence of dimerization and trimerization in 2D hydrogen and helium systems with various interactions, thereby supporting findings from a recent publication. Conversely, the study identifies the existence of Pauli-induced trimerization and dimerization under specified conditions.

This study introduces Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN) as a tool for resolving time-varying matrix problems, such as finding a pseudoinverse for a matrix that changes over time. Although ZNN was initially developed in 1992, it has not been thoroughly explored in the literature, and several key aspects of the method remain unclear. In this research, a comprehensive overview of ZNN is provided, including its mathematical foundation and coding implementation in C/C++. Furthermore, the paper showcases the effectiveness of C/C++-based ZNN in solving a pseudoinverse problem for a dynamically changing matrix, influenced by random noise, and highlights how adjusting the rate of state convergence can improve the accuracy of the solution.

A prevalent characteristic in biological vision systems is the on-off center-surround receptive field, which is known to be effective in extracting edges and reducing noise. This study develops a classification algorithm incorporating an on-off center-surround receptive field, which is unique in its bidirectional, non-linear response to light. The non-linear response enables the model to efficiently capture contrast information, which is crucial for distinguishing between light and dark areas in images, particularly in low-light conditions. The proposed method demonstrates enhanced accuracy and robustness in image classification tasks, especially when dealing with low-light images, as evidenced by the model's superior performance on the LSUN-Bedrooms dataset, which outperforms state-of-the-art models in a low-light environment.

Our paper presents an algorithm to optimize wide-field X-ray telescope mirrors, where the conventional approach of manually selecting mirror parameters is often insufficient to achieve optimal performance. The proposed algorithm employs numerical optimization techniques to automate the selection process and can be applied to Wolter I, II, and III designs. The optimization process focuses on key performance metrics, such as effective area, field of view, and image quality, and our results indicate that this approach can yield significant improvements over traditional methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm can be used to optimize mirror configurations for specific metrics, such as the 80 percent encircled energy fraction at a certain angular radius. The algorithm can also be used to optimize mirror shapes beyond traditional shapes, such as free-form or non-rotationally symmetric mirrors, and we provide numerical examples to illustrate its effectiveness in these scenarios.

The core principle of the magnetic Bloch theorem is that under a quantized flux of $2\pi$, the electronic properties of twisted bilayer graphene revert to those found in isolated layers of bil graphene. The primary finding of this study is that when the magnetic field is aligned perpendicular to the plane, the flat bands in this twisted structure disappear at the threshold of $2\pi$ flux. The flat bands in the structure are found to be on the verge of a Lifshitz phase transition, where they vanish as they approach this threshold. The twist angle of $1.1^{\circ}$ in the twisted structure is found to be very close to the $2\pi$ flux condition, and when the magnetic field is applied, the electronic properties of the structure are found to be similar to that of a bil graphene structure. The interlayer interactions in the twisted structure are found to be the primary factor that determines the electronic properties, and when the magnetic field is applied, the electronic properties of the structure are found to be similar to that of a bil graphene structure. The structure is found to have a rich electronic properties that can be controlled by the twist angle, the magnetic field, and the Fermi energy.

Inspired by a desire to create a secure, high-capacity communication system with friends, I embarked on a project to develop a natural language steganography tool. This process involved designing an LSTM-based model that could conceal a predetermined secret message within the text output generated by the model. Before commencing the research, I conducted an examination of existing literature on natural language steganography, revealing a significant gap in published studies. Following a thorough literature review, I implemented the proposed model using the Coarse-to-Fine Learning approach, which demonstrated its effectiveness in concealing a secret message within the generated text. Notably, the StegonLP model exhibited the ability to successfully hide a secret message while maintaining high perplexity and a low detection rate in comparison to a baseline.

The unit commitment problem is a fundamental issue in power systems, and its optimal solution is crucial for systems' economic and reliable operation. Researchers have developed various techniques to tackle this problem, including the constraint screening method which can significantly reduce computational time. This paper introduces a machine learning-based cost model for screening constraints, utilizing the model to estimate generator costs and identify those with the lowest operational expenses. By integrating this approach with the constraint screening method, this research demonstrates a substantial improvement in computational efficiency, with a 10-fold reduction in computational time for a specific power system test case.

Research on the data from single crystals of alpha-Li2IrO3, conducted under high pressure up to 14 GPa using Raman spectroscopy, revealed that pressure causes a significant shift in certain vibrational modes. This shift indicates that pressure induces dimerization of Ir ions in the material, with its critical dimerization pressure being lower than that in Na2IrO3. Under high pressure, antiferromagnetic behavior in alpha-Li2IrO3 is suppressed, with both materials sharing a similar transition pressure where this occurs. This finding suggests that a specific structural arrangement and similar spin interactions in alpha-Li2IrO3 lead to comparable pressure responses as seen in Na2IrO3, despite the latter having an additional J' interaction.

In situations where randomized trials are not feasible, researchers often rely on observational data to draw conclusions about causal effects. One prominent method used in such cases is the difference-in-differences (DiD) estimator. However, the validity of DiD relies on the assumption of parallel trends, which cannot be verified empirically. This limitation becomes particularly problematic when units are added or removed from a dataset, rendering DiD estimates unreliable. This study introduces a novel approach called synthetic controls (SC) to address this issue by creating synthetic control groups with units that exhibit parallel trends in pre-intervention periods. SC allows for valid causal inferences without verifying parallel trends by incorporating additional pre-intervention data points. This research develops a novel theoretical framework to support the validity of SC by utilizing proximal causal inference methods. This new framework enhances the robustness of causal inferences by providing empirical evidence for parallel trends through auxiliary data. SC unit value regression discontinuity designs are also considered within this framework. This comprehensive approach is complemented by rigorous theoretical findings, which demonstrate the asymptotic normality of SC DiD DiD estimators under various assumptions. This research provides a theoretical foundation for future studies to build upon and apply DiD and SC designs in a broader range of contexts.

Using graph neural networks, researchers have achieved significant advancements in graph machine learning. The growing interest in private graph data has led to the development of private algorithms for specific tasks. However, comparing the topological differences between two graphs in a distributed setting while preserving privacy remains an unresolved issue. In this research, we introduce a novel private algorithm designed to estimate the discrepancy between the topological structures of graphs from distinct populations. The proposed algorithm combines local differential privacy with dimensionality reduction techniques to estimate the discrepancy between graphs' optimal transport maps. Our findings demonstrate that the discrepancy between the estimated and true discrepancy values decreases at a specific rate as the sample size increases. The method's effectiveness is further demonstrated through numerical experiments using synthetic data, revealing its superiority over existing public benchmark methods.

The dynamics of self-focusing and self-modulation of intense laser pulses in plasma are influenced by nonlinearity arising from the plasma's ion density modulation. This effect is analyzed in the context of intense laser pulses undergoing self-steepening and leading to the formation of intense sub-pulses at the trailing edge. The interaction of such sub-pulses with overcritical plasma results in a modulated relativistic foot, which can be significantly amplified and potentially accelerated by the sub-pulse itself. The relationship between the laser pulse's initial polarization and the structure of the modulated foot is investigated, with findings suggesting that a polarized foot can be utilized to control the injection and acceleration of electrons.

A platinum foil with a mass of 10 grams was used in a 100 kilovolt-pandimensional time-proportional counter experiment to set limits on various processes related to double beta decay and particle dark matter. By analyzing the collected data, researchers found the most stringent limits on dark matter-induced effects, including those related to neutrinoless double beta decay and particle interactions with germanium, resulting in a change in the effective neutrino mass. By considering a combination of factors, including gamma radiation and particle interactions with germanium, researchers found a lower bound of 9.1 x 10^-13 for one process and 9.1 x 10^-13 for another. Additionally, researchers found a limit on another process, resulting in a limit of 9.1 x 10^-13 for one isotope and 9.1 x 10^-13 for another isotope.

The value of the renormalization constant $Z_J$ for the flavor-singlet axial-vector current $J_5$ is crucial for determining the nucleon's axial and pseudoscalar matrix elements, which are key to understanding the anomaly contribution to the proton's spin and the transition form factor between the proton and the pseudoscalar meson. As a dimension-3 operator in quantum chromodynamics, $Z_{J_5}$ is a multiplicative renormalization constant. Our study aims to determine $Z_{J_5}$ in the $N_f=3$ version of the standard dimensional regularization scheme, specifically in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme to two-loop order.

This study introduces an innovative application of colorization, termed cross-camera colorization, a task with two primary objectives. The first goal is to restore a low-resolution, single-view grayscale image captured from a different camera, distinct from the high-resolution color images in the training set, with various color styles. The second goal is to identify and apply an appropriate color style from the high-resolution images, allowing users to choose a desired colorization effect. To achieve this, a novel transformer-based architecture, StyleCrossCamera, is proposed. The architecture employs a grayscale image encoder, a style selector that chooses the desired color style, and a color image decoder to generate the cross-camera colorized result. Additionally, the StyleCrossCamera architecture is extended to incorporate low-resolution images. The proposed approach is evaluated on an established single-view colorization dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing high-quality colorized results.

This study focuses on expanding the understood ergodic motion of the $n$-dimensional Ermakov system by establishing its broader symmetry and conservation law properties. The findings demonstrate that a 2-parameter Lie point symmetry is a subset of Noether's symmetry within the Lagrangian system, with the associated conservation law being the weak form of Noether's theorem's conservation law. The study also presents the general form of Noether's conservation law and a method to generate an infinite number of conserved quantities from the general form and the 2-parameter symmetry generator. The researchers apply this method to derive infinite conservation laws for the $n$-dimensional Ermakov system and provide several examples to validate the findings.

Public transportation agencies worldwide utilize the Feed Specification Encoding Format (FST) for data exchange and management. However, due to its large and complex nature, many agencies struggle to process and provide it as a public good. Historically, agential decisions have driven a lack of focus on making public transportation data accessible. To address this issue and unlock the potential of smart city initiatives, our research introduces a new data-driven approach that utilizes recurrent neural networks to process and predict unavailable transit data in FST format. By converting FST data into a more manageable binary state, our model is able to analyze historical patterns and predict future movements of public transportation vehicles. Through comprehensive experiments using real-world data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately predicting public transportation movements and increasing data accessibility.

To address the issue of learning effective class-level prototypes for few-shot learning, we propose an approach that involves optimizing a prototype network with a separability objective function. This method aims to produce well-separated prototypes that can be used for few-shot learning tasks. Our results show that the prototype network produces better performance than traditional few-shot base models across various datasets, particularly when using larger numbers of query samples. Additionally, we found that the best results can be achieved by using a combination of the prototype network and few-shot base models.

We're investigating a specific instance of Goldstone's theorem, specifically for non-invertible continuous symmetries, and we're working within the framework of effective field theories. In the process, we'll develop a Lagrangian for a theory featuring a non-local conserved current, and we'll analyze how this current relates to primary operators within a Conformal Field Theory. Additionally, we'll explore a scenario where space is compactified, and we'll investigate a 1D system, ultimately laying the groundwork for analyzing non-invertible higher-form symmetries.

A semi-transitive graph is a directed graph that avoids certain patterns, specifically transitive cycles, a certain type of cycle with an additional edge, and cycles of a certain length. This paper addresses the semi-transitive orientability of split graphs and shows that a split graph is semi-transitically orientable if and only if its tournament hosts neither a specific cycle pattern nor a cycle with an additional edge in which the path has two forward edges. Additionally, the paper provides a linear-time algorithm for determining the semi-transitive orientability of a split graph.

A cutting-edge method is introduced for detecting hadronic tau decays within the CMS experiment's calorimeter and particle-flow system. By utilizing the tau's distinctive characteristics, such as a lower invariant mass, fewer particles, and an asymmetric energy spread, a 10-layer fully connected neural network is developed. This network effectively differentiates between tau decays and background events from jets and leptonic decays. By training the network with fixed jet and lepton momenta, a comprehensive deep neural network classifier is established for the exclusion of untagged events. As a result, the classifier achieves impressive performance, offering background rejection powers of 10 to 100 at tagger efficiencies of 30-50%, thereby enhancing the sensitivity of hadronic final states in searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

Future sky surveys from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory will generate massive amounts of multi-wavelength data, including precise astrometry and photometry, which will be crucial for understanding the universe's most significant phenomena. However, the resulting data will be plagued by noise and systematic errors, making it essential to develop advanced machine learning techniques for accurate object classification. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) can provide uncertainty estimates, making them suitable for this purpose. This study evaluates the effectiveness of BNNs in solving complex classification problems, using a combination of astrometric and photometric data from the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. By comparing BNNs with traditional maximum-likelihood methods and exploring the impact of different network architectures, we demonstrate that BNNs can outperform traditional methods in certain scenarios, especially when dealing with uncertain data. This research contributes to the development of machine learning tools for the upcoming era of big data in astronomy.

Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering between different modal paths in a solid-core photonic crystal fiber, a process that is significantly more impactful than modal Brillouin scattering. By utilizing a five-hole design, we have been able to observe intermodal Brillouin scattering events involving the fundamental mode and higher-order modes, specifically the LP11 and LP21 modes. These events exhibit distinct characteristics, with varying frequencies and strengths. Moreover, we have established a correlation between the mechanical properties of the fiber and the characteristics of this scattering process.

In 1996, Dyer established a crucial theorem which enabled the creation of the Dyer-Mohanty algorithm for calculating the y-vectors of reflections in types A and B. Nearly two decades later, a more comprehensive version of this theorem was proposed in relation to the Brown-Hudson generators for Coxeter groups of type B and D, and this theory was fully developed and proven in this paper, along with a comprehensive generalization of the y-vector computation algorithm for these groups.

Two specific types of knapsack problems, known as Set-Union Knapsack and Budgeted Maximum Coverage, are variations of the classic Knapsack problem. The classic problem aims to find the best combination of items within a given budget, whereas these more complex problems aim to achieve the best outcome by grouping items into sets and considering the cost of each set. The objective of the paper is to develop efficient local search methods for solving these complex knapsack problems. The authors propose local search algorithms that use a combination of swapping and shifting strategies, and demonstrate through extensive numerical experiments that these algorithms are highly effective, with the most advanced variant outperforming the current best heuristic methods by a significant margin, achieving the best results in 95% of the test cases.

Churn prediction is a critical challenge in online businesses, and it's particularly significant in the online gambling industry. In this research, we introduce a novel Churn Index (CI) to forecast churn in this sector. Our proposed CI is based on the time intervals between a player's consecutive wagers, and it's calculated using the decayed cumulative mean of these time intervals. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using real-world data from an online gambling platform.

The investigation of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in 2D Ising field theory with a magnetic field focuses on understanding its edge singularity edge point at $H=-h_{0}$, where $h_{0}>0$. This point is characterized by a vanishing magnetic field and complex analysis techniques. It has been theoretically established that the renormalized magnetic field is zero and a non-zero renormalized magnetic susceptibility exponent $\sigma$ occurs. This outcome is consistent with a conformal field theory with central charge $c=-2/5$ and magnetic field turned off, as well as recent numerical simulations and experiments.

Our research develops a framework for calculating transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions (TMDPDFs) at leading order using large-momentum effective theory (LaMET). We demonstrate that TMDPDFs can be factorized into separate functions that depend on individual transverse momenta and are multiplied by a momentum-dependent coefficient, or Wilson line. We derive a novel evolution equation that describes how these functions change with energy scale. This equation is validated by comparing it with an established formalism. Our analysis includes a calculation of the gluon's transverse momentum-dependent function in proton kinematics at next-to-leading order in perturbation theory. Wilson lines are shown to be expressible as simple combinations of simpler building blocks. Our work provides a foundation for future computational advancements in the field.

In the collisions of ultra-relativistic heavy ions that occur without actual impact, a process called ultra-peripheral collision takes place, resulting in the interaction of leptons with heavy nuclei through electromagnetic forces. These forces are extremely intense, allowing them to cause significant effects on the motion of charged particles. Specifically, the electromagnetic field generated by a heavy nucleus can become distorted by the presence of a virtual pair of charged particles, ultimately leading to observable changes in the motion of a single electron or positron. Researchers have studied the electromagnetic interaction between high-energy particles and heavy ions in the context of ultra-peripheral collisions, focusing on the formation of positronium atoms and the potential for electromagnetic energy loss. Their analysis has shown that the interaction between a high-energy particle and a heavy ion can lead to the emission of energy through the absorption of the particle by the ionic core, ultimately resulting in a measurable effect on the motion of the particle.

To enhance cyclist safety, there is a pressing need to develop advanced warning systems that can significantly reduce accidents and preventable injuries. Focusing on urban environments, this research aims to create a groundbreaking method for assessing accident risks for cyclists. Our innovative approach involves using a wearable camera to capture video footage, which is then analyzed to identify potential hazards. Our experiments involved 25 participants navigating urban areas, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm in accurately detecting risks. Moreover, this research paves the way for developing sophisticated systems capable of communicating with other cyclists and smart infrastructure, ultimately fostering a collaborative environment for improved safety.

A novel method for creating safety assurance systems and robust navigation strategies is introduced, utilizing control barrier functions to handle the uncertainties inherent in robotic movements. The proposed approach, centered around a robust optimal navigation system integrated with a model predictive controller, prioritizes safety by using a priority queue-based method to maintain the controller's stability. Extensive simulations involving mobile and humanoid robots demonstrate the method's capacity to effectively mitigate uncertainties and plan safe movements.

A subset S of a finite ring R is considered self-covering if the product of any two elements in S, denoted as [S,S], covers R along with at least one non-zero element from the ring's Jacobson radical. Researchers have investigated the existence of self-covering sets with a particular size threshold, such as the covering number $\gamma(R)$, the smallest cardinality of a self-covering subset in ring R. Studies have shown that for certain rings, like $\mathbb{Z}_n$, a self-covering subset with a quarter of the ring's size exists, but for other rings, a self-covering subset can exceed half the ring's size, and in some cases, it can be as high as 9/10 of the ring's size.

Deep neural networks are highly susceptible to subtle, malicious alterations in their input images, known as adversarial examples. In response, numerous defenses have been developed, but many are essentially ad-hoc measures. In this research, we examine the natural properties of deep learning models and their resistance to such attacks. By using images in their original format, without any data augmentation or preprocessing, we found that certain deep neural networks are surprisingly resilient to adversarial examples. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a diverse range of colors in the input image contributes to this natural resistance, and even simply rotating the image 90 degrees can significantly reduce the effects of the malicious alterations. These results suggest that incorporating color diversity and appropriate data handling can enhance the natural robustness of deep neural networks to adversarial examples.

The nonlocal conservation laws we analyze are nonlinear equations that model various forms of traffic flow, including those with time-dependent and nonlocal flux functions based on different types of data. In particular, we demonstrate the stability of solutions in the case where the flux function is not smooth, having a singularity at zero. The stability of these solutions is also confirmed by showing that they satisfy an entropy inequality for a specific convex entropy function. Furthermore, in the case where the flux function is smooth, we show that the solutions of these nonlocal equations converge to the unique entropy-admissible solution of a corresponding local conservation law as the nonlocal scale approaches zero. The speed of this convergence is shown to be proportional to the square root of the nonlocal scale.

Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow their local geometric transformations to include both translation and scaling, making them intrinsically linked to affine structures. Utilizing a key property, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of dilation surfaces with specific, simplified flow patterns, characterized by isolated flow points and non-crossing saddle points, on all given surfaces with a valid dilation structure. Slightly expanding the dilation condition, we derive similar results for a broader class of surfaces with defined affine structures, including translation surfaces, which are characterized by parallel parallel transport and zero curvature.

Recent studies have highlighted the limitations of traditional correlation measures in analyzing complex data sets, leading to the development of alternative measures like total correlation. This concept has been applied to studying brain connectivity using resting-state fMRI scans, where existing studies rely on traditional correlation measures. This study compares the effectiveness of total correlation and Pearson correlation in defining brain networks, revealing that total correlation outperforms Pearson correlation due to its ability to capture complex dependencies between brain regions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of estimating total correlation from data using a method based on mutual information, and we apply this approach to analyze the human connectome, yielding a more comprehensive understanding of brain organization compared to traditional correlation measures.

The Taylor isomorphism connecting Clifford algebra functions to the Segal-Bargmann space is enhanced by extending it to Clifford algebra-valued functions and introducing a new transform, which also reveals the unitary nature of the original Taylor isomorphism.

We are going to develop a general approach for computing Gaussian processes' conditional distributions, focusing on providing numerically stable algorithms for their evaluation. This approach will be applied to several special cases, including Gaussian processes with zero mean, governed by stochastic differential equations. Additionally, the stochastic nature of Gaussian processes pathwise conditioning will be explored, and the associated implications discussed.

This research examines the wireless coverage of a terrestrial sensor network operating at a single frequency. To ensure seamless connectivity, additional aerial sensors are introduced to bridge any isolated terrestrial sensor groups. The optimal placement of these airborne nodes is determined by solving a specific optimization problem, which is then compared with the equivalent problem of connectivity using single-hop wireless coverage. To validate the proposed approach, an efficient algorithm is developed for sensor placement, which is shown to be effective in maximizing long-term network performance.

The DUNE experiment, a pioneering effort in long-baseline neutrino physics, is set to take place at the International Large Detector facility in the US. Utilizing a high-energy neutrino and antineutrino beam, the experiment will examine the neutrino octet, revealing the absolute neutrino mass hierarchy, measuring CP-violating phases in the lepton sector, and determining neutrino mixing parameters. Additionally, the experiment will investigate neutrino interactions, search for unknown physics, and study astrophysical neutrinos. This paper will provide an overview of the DUNE experiment's scientific objectives, current status, and future plans.

Research into top tagging using XGBoost and interpreting its results through 
normalized Shapley values, with applications in boosted tagging improved by such 
methods, have been conducted.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for virtual organizations, requirement refinement, abstractions of models, and concrete instantiations. The document also examines Virtual Organizations within these contexts.

To improve the sample efficiency of policy optimization, we introduce a variance reduction technique using experience replay. Our approach, built upon the natural policy gradient, combines selective experience replay with covariance matrix trace adaptation. Based on the online mirror descent framework, these innovations contribute to significantly reducing the variance of the gradient estimate. Our theoretical analysis confirms the effectiveness of this method, yielding improved time complexity and a linear convergence rate for logistic policy gradients. Furthermore, empirical evaluations demonstrate the practical benefits of this policy gradient solution.

Two distinct methods, termed the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula, have been developed to integrate certain classes of supermatrix integrals. In this study, we demonstrate the equivalence of these methods, proving that they yield the same result. The proof relies on a straightforward derivation, utilizing the initial superbosonization formula and demonstrating its derivation from the GHS transformation. Furthermore, several new identities related to supermatrices are presented as a consequence of this proof, along with an application of these findings to supergroup integrals.

In the field of forecasting, spatio-temporal learning is gaining significant attention due to its practical applications. However, existing models often overlook crucial details about movement, which are particularly important in fields like traffic prediction. To address this limitation, a new approach called MoDeRNN has been developed. This model focuses on the intrinsic characteristics of objects and their movement patterns to enhance the accuracy of predictions. By incorporating local and global motion features, MoDeRNN enables a more nuanced understanding of the data. Furthermore, the integration of these features allows for the creation of a more granular module that can be applied to various types of data. Experimental results have demonstrated MoDeRTNN's effectiveness and adaptability across multiple datasets and prediction tasks.

We introduce Josephine, a JavaScript library that leverages WebAssembly to utilize Rust's safety features, specifically focusing on data ownership and lifetime management. By utilizing Rust's Drop trait, Josephine ensures the lifespan of data within WebAssembly applications, while also allowing access to JavaScript memory through controlled pointers and references, represented by the JPointer and JRef types. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Josephine in utilizing Rust's performance features, such as direct JavaScript memory access and reference counting, in the context of image processing, specifically in the manipulation of pixel arrays, which are accessed via pointer and reference types.

The search for neutrinoless double-beta decay is a crucial method for proving that neutrinos have mass and determining the mass of light neutrinos through a precise measurement known as the neutrino effective mass. Researchers have found discrepancies between the neutrino effective mass and data from beta decay experiments, suggesting the need for a revised understanding. A possible explanation could be that current experiments are measuring an average over distinct decay pathways, each corresponding to a specific neutrino mass eigenstate. To investigate this theory, researchers have explored the concept of 'neutrinoless double-beta decay at colliders', a novel approach proposed by the author that allows for a clearer distinction between contributing neutrino mass eigenstates and can potentially resolve existing discrepancies.

This paper introduces an iterative polar code decoding technique called the partial decimation with polar decoding (PDPD) strategy. The PDPD method is a hybrid of channel polarization and belief propagation list decoding. It is characterized by a high level of error correction capability, yet it is more complex than standard list decoding. The PDPD technique achieves better error correction performance than conventional list decoding, while maintaining comparable decoding delay. Furthermore, the PDPD method outperforms the fixed cutoff weight list decoding (FCWL) method in both error correction performance and decoding delay. The analysis of the PDPD method is based on the derivation of its error correction performance bounds and the characterization of its code distance properties. The study also explores the relationship between the PDPD method and the polar code distance, providing new insights into the error correction performance of polar codes.

When combining multiple astronomical images, a common practice is to create a single, more sensitive image by stacking them together. In this paper, a mathematical expression for the Point Spread Function (PSF) of a coadded image is developed, assuming that the individual images have Gaussian-distributed PSFs. The derived formula for the coadded PSF is valid for images that are combined with equal exposure times and those that have different PSF widths. A corresponding expression for the variance of the coadded image's pixel values is also established. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the coadded PSF can be effectively represented as a sum of two Gaussian functions, with the relative importance of each depending on the sensitivity of the images being combined.

This paper explores the fracture toughness of a solid through numerical simulations.  We create a fracture energy score for each bond in a single crystal by measuring how much the bond is stretched, focusing on tensile strain.  Through simulations of pre-cracked squares and cubes with different crystal shapes under increasing pressure, we find that the solid's stress decreases after reaching a peak and then gradually drops.  By analyzing this stress drop, we're able to calculate the fracture toughness of different solids.  Our results show that the fracture toughness is influenced by the solid's geometry, but not by the size of the sample.  We also find that the stress drop is caused by a bond breaking when it reaches a certain strain threshold, and that this bond's energy is equal to the fracture energy of the solid.  Through further simulations, we confirm that the fracture energy of the solid is equal to twice the fracture energy of a single bond.  Our results also show that the fracture toughness of the solid is equal to the yield stress of the solid multiplied by the fracture energy of the solid, divided by the atomic spacing of the solid.  Our findings also indicate that the fracture toughness of the solid is equal to the fracture toughness of a single bond multiplied by a geometric factor that depends on the shape of the solid.  Our simulations also show that the fracture toughness of the solid is equal to the fracture toughness of a single bond multiplied by a factor that depends on the orientation of the bond in the solid.  Our

This paper presents the first instance of coupling the Gaussian free field with the Loewen function, the driven SLE and the Brownian motion SLE, within the context of the upper half-plane. To achieve this, a new approach is introduced, enabling the derivation of the cross-section law of Brownian motion SLEs through the stochastic log-gas probability distribution. This breakthrough facilitates the development of the cross-section law of Schramm-Loewner evolution driven by stochastic cross-sections of the Gaussian free field.

In this study, we derive precise upper limits for the H^s norm of 3D incompressible fluid flow, described by the Navier-Stokes equations with periodic initial conditions. Our analysis shows that this estimate depends directly on the initial conditions, the wavenumber, and some physical constants. Building on this result, we also establish corresponding estimates for the heat equation and the heat equation with fractional Laplacian.

In the context of verifying quantum computation outcomes, a classical device aims to confirm the result of a quantum algorithm without replicating its complexity. This task is significant, particularly when the quantum result is uncertain or the quantum device is untrusted. The approach involves the verifier interacting with the quantum device through a single entangled quantum memory, allowing the verifier to track the quantum state's evolution without needing substantial computational resources. This method is demonstrated to be effective even when the quantum algorithm includes an uncertain quantum step, and it is shown that this method requires the verifier to process information at a rate proportional to the algorithm's size. Furthermore, this method is applicable when the quantum device uses a matrix-based approach, allowing the verifier to question the quantum device at a randomly selected point in time. This method is also applicable when the quantum device uses a matrix-based approach, allowing the verifier to track the quantum state's evolution through local operations.

A significant portion of the global population is affected by food insecurity, with one-third of all food items being wasted.  The complex nature of the food industry, which is heavily regulated, has led to numerous instances of contamination and spoilage.  These issues can be minimized by implementing a transparent and accountable supply chain, which can be achieved through the adoption of advanced technologies.  In this paper, we propose a solution to the challenges within the food industry by introducing a blockchain-based architecture, supported by the MEGA framework, which enables the creation of smart contracts and the integration of IoT devices and services.  Our proposed architecture enables the development of a blockchain-based system, which can track and monitor the food supply chain, thereby reducing waste and improving transparency and accountability.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed solution through the development of a case study, which showcases the potential of blockchain-based systems to address the regulatory and transparency issues within the food industry.

This research introduces a novel generative model, combining self-supervision and implicit representations, to create realistic living cell shapes. The proposed model, called CellNet, employs shape nets, a type of implicit representation, to parameterize cell boundaries. By leveraging data from diverse cell types, CellNet can generate synthetic cells that accurately mimic the size, area-to-perimeter ratio, and morphological features of real cells. The model's generative capabilities are assessed through visual and statistical analyses, and CellNet's potential applications in understanding cell morphology and biological function are discussed.

Blind and low-vision individuals frequently struggle to navigate documents, 
particularly those created by older individuals who often have limited computer skills.
As researchers investigating these users' document navigation abilities, we discovered 
that existing assistive technologies are inadequate in facilitating effective 
navigation. Our study aims to uncover the unique challenges these users face and 
identify their specific needs, which will ultimately inform the development of more 
user-friendly navigation tools.

Recent studies have developed pre-trained language models that outperform BERT on multiple tasks by employing decoder architectures and incorporating positional embeddings. However, using positional embeddings limits the information the model can obtain from previous tokens in sequences, and the use of masked language modeling (MLM) in BERT may lead to training inconsistencies. To address these limitations, XLNet combines predictive language modeling and permutation aggregation, and removes the need for special tokens and masks. This results in a more accurate and efficient model that achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on 16 out of 17 GLUE benchmarks.

The advancement of powerful instruments like the High Resolution Spectrographs (HRG) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has significantly improved our ability to analyze the atmospheres of exoplanets. However, stellar activity poses a significant challenge to precise spectroscopic analysis. In this study, we examine how stellar activity impacts the analysis of low-resolution spectra and the role of high-resolution spectra in mitigating this impact. We found that the chromosphere of a star can contribute to the transit spectra of planets, particularly in the case of bright stars like Kepler-138. We also found that high-resolution spectra can be used to distinguish between the effects of a planet's atmosphere and those of a star's activity. By analyzing the spectral patterns and amplitudes, we were able to identify the effects of a planet's atmosphere and those of a star's activity. This research provides new insights into the analysis of exoplanet atmospheres and highlights the importance of considering stellar activity in this process.

Our approach to constructing a conformal metric on a Riemann surface with singularities draws from an elliptic equation whose solution depends on the surface's metric and a function describing the singularities' angles. This method's validity relies on established results by Nirenberg and a result from Poincaré equations on surfaces with degenerate metrics. Additionally, our analysis incorporates a spherical metric on the Riemann surface, leading to a simplified solution for a function with zero total "charge" or a spherical metric when the singularities' angles sum to an even multiple of $2\pi$.

Our research focuses on the swimming mechanics of the centipede species *Scutigera coleopodina*, which can traverse on the water's surface using leg movements. Through high-speed video analysis, we found that the centipedes create thrust primarily with their front legs and maintain stability using rear legs. Our force measurements revealed that the centipedes exploit a combination of drag and surface tension to achieve a speed of 0.17 m/s. Furthermore, our observations revealed that the centipedes exhibit a unique undulating motion, similar to fish, when swimming in the water. Our findings reveal that the centipede's surface swimming style shares similarities with the surface skimming techniques used by insects, while its underwater propulsion method mirrors that of fish.

The study of asteroid impacts on planetary bodies is a crucial aspect of planetary science, yet it remains a complex and computationally demanding process. This study focuses on developing high-resolution simulation techniques for the analysis of wave-like tsunami propagation triggered by such impacts. To achieve this, we employ an advanced numerical model that leverages adaptive grid refinement to increase precision where it's most needed. Our results, which involve running simulations on a planet similar to Mars, show that this approach can produce highly detailed predictions of impact-generated tsunamis, paving the way for more efficient and accurate planetary impact studies.

A newly identified population of distant galaxies is emerging, consisting of small, low-mass systems that radiate intense infrared energy. These galaxies, which we call IRBODGs, are distinct from previously known massive, star-forming objects at the same redshift. We have discovered a large number of these galaxies using the NIRCam instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope. These galaxies are characterized by their lack of a strong 6-micron emission and moderate dust content, which is consistent with a young age and a lack of older stars. We have also found that the galaxies' star formation rates are lower than previously estimated from their infrared energy, which is consistent with a population of young, low-mass galaxies. These galaxies are now being used to study the star formation history of the universe at high redshift.

We investigate how the gravity sector in seven-dimensional supergravity theories,
containing distinct topological terms, influences the field theory content when
the manifold is reduced to a torus. By analyzing this, we establish a connection
between the topological components of seven-dimensional gravity and the Chern-Simons
form in abelian three-form field theory, leading to the creation of a one-form
potential current algebra. This finding is then used to derive a term in the action
principle of chiral three-form fields on the three-sphere.

In a long, narrow, and closed container, a collection of randomly distributed disks of varying sizes and weights is present. When a specific number of disks of one type is introduced, researchers have found the jammed packing jamunot to exhibit periodic patterns. These patterns, known as jamunot, are similar to the packing patterns of jamunot formed by disks of a single type. The study of this system has led to a deeper understanding of the complex patterns of disk packings, particularly when two types of disks are involved. The researchers have found that the probability of disk A appearing in a jamunot is directly related to its number fraction, fA, and that the period of jamunot is equal to 2fA + 1. The study of this system has led to a deeper understanding of the complex patterns of disk packings, particularly when two types of disks are involved. To better understand how El Nino and La Nina cycles affect global precipitation patterns, researchers analyzed historical precipitation data from the period 1980-2019. By categorizing El Nino cycles into two types - traditional and positive high latitude - they found significant differences in their impacts on precipitation. Specifically, the positive high latitude type was linked to increased precipitation in the tropics and decreased precipitation in the extratropics, whereas the traditional type resulted in decreased precipitation in the tropics and increased precipitation in the extratropics. The positive high latitude type also exhibited a more pronounced effect in the extratropical regions. In contrast, the traditional type was found to be more closely related to the strength of the El Nino event, whereas the positive high latitude type was not. On the other hand, La Nina events were found to exhibit similar impacts on precipitation at similar latitudes but with opposite signs, and the La Nino positive high latitude type was found to exhibit decreased precipitation in the tropics and increased precipitation in the extratropics, whereas the La Nino traditional type resulted in increased precipitation in the tropics and decreased precipitation in the extratropical regions.

A new technique for analyzing the expansion characteristics of foams and honeycombs is introduced, allowing for the examination of their growth patterns at a micro-level. Experimental evidence from decompressing foams and foams subjected to shear forces shows that their expansion behavior can be quantified. Additionally, our findings confirm that these materials maintain a consistent level of non-affine behavior, independent of their porosity or shear strain. Furthermore, our research provides insights into how individual cells within the foam expand and how this is related to their overall shape.

This research focuses on developing single-species population models that consider the effects of aging, population density, and psychological impact. The models are categorized into three distinct types based on their growth patterns: exponential, logistic, and Alle-Kerrich. The study employs the discrete-time Lotka model to analyze the dynamics of these populations and seeks to identify conditions that lead to stable, positive solutions. The outcome of this analysis reveals the existence of a stable equilibrium and the stability of the model's solutions. Furthermore, the research examines the long-term behavior of the model's solutions and investigates how changes in the distribution of aging times affect the model's outcomes. The findings of this study are then applied to the specific examples of the discrete-time Lotka model, distinguishing the model's behavior in different time intervals.

The researchers investigate the characteristics of hypersequential presentations of logics based on substructural logic, focusing on those that allow weakening and contraction. They establish a criterion for the decidability of such logics and create a method for determining the upper complexity limits of valid proofs in the hypersequent framework. By applying this approach, they derive the exact complexity limits for several well-known logics, including the full hypersequent version of the logic LP, the logic KMM, and the full hypersequent version of the logic MTL.

Hierarchical taxonomies, such as product categories, are effectively modeled using the tree structure in hyperbolic space due to their inherent natural hierarchy. Enhancing taxonomies through the addition of relevant terms improves search functionality and the overall user experience. However, the difficulty lies in identifying suitable terms that fit within the existing taxonomy structure. Traditional learning methods, which rely on Euclidean geometry, may not adequately capture the complex hierarchical relationships necessary for this purpose. A novel approach, HyperExpan, utilizes a hyperbolic tensor decomposition framework to optimize the learning process and ensure that the refined taxonomy maintains its hierarchical structure within the hyperbolic manifold. By incorporating hyperbolic projections of word and taxonomy embeddings, HyperExpan identifies and ranks relevant terms for each category, resulting in a more accurate and comprehensive taxonomy. Empirical tests confirm HyperExpan's superiority over its Euclidean counterpart and the state-of-the-art linear expansion method.

This research examines how dimer-monomer complexes of the molecular S66 channel respond to electric fields. We utilize quantum chemical methods to analyze charge transfer and polarization within dimers composed of six distinct base pairs, including urea, water, and 2-hydroxybenzoic acid molecules. When exposed to electric fields, these dimers exhibit increased stability, as evidenced by their elevated interaction energies and decreased intermolecular distances. Notably, the urea dimer demonstrates the most significant response to the electric field, displaying a substantial increase in interaction energy and a corresponding reduction in the distance between its constituent molecules. Furthermore, our results reveal that the orientation of dimers significantly influences their response to the electric field. Notably, dimers with parallel orientations exhibit the most pronounced response to the electric field. This research provides valuable insights into the behavior of dimer complexes in the presence of electric fields, which may have significant implications for understanding the behavior of molecular systems in the human body.

The fourth Industrial Revolution has greatly impacted manufacturing systems, particularly scheduling. Modern scheduling approaches utilize data from various sources to make informed decisions, but many fail to acknowledge the inherent uncertainty in this data. As a result, these decision-making processes can be compromised. This research examines the impact of uncertainty in Industry 4.0 scheduling and presents a novel method to incorporate probabilistic information into decision-making. We employ the SEPALE algorithm to tackle the complex scheduling problem involving uncertain processing times and dynamic customer orders. By comparing our approach with industry-standard scheduling methods, the study demonstrates the potential benefits of uncertainty modeling in improving decision-making within Industry 4.0 systems.

Cyber-Physical Systems are increasingly vulnerable to malicious attacks, which can disrupt their operational stability, prompting a need for resilience measures. To address this concern, a formal approach is presented for quantifying the robustness of Cyber-Physical Systems against cyber attacks. This method utilizes a specific type of logical expression, known as Sign-LTL, to describe operational stability and incorporates logical operators that account for uncertainty in observational data. By formulating resilience measures based on this formal expression, we can evaluate and compare theoretical and practical instances of Cyber-Physical Systems to determine their theoretical resilience capabilities and actual resilience performance.

A novel search strategy for dark matter is introduced, leveraging the sensitivity of modern MEMS accelerometers to minute forces within a global network. This approach targets fermionic dark matter with masses within a specific sub-Hz range, where its oscillations produce detectable accelerations as per the Einstein Equivalence Principle. A global network of accelerometers can distinguish between dark matter signals and potential noise sources, effectively isolating the former. With a large-scale deployment of high-sensitivity instruments, this method offers the first direct dark matter detection in the specified mass range, with unique predictions that can be empirically validated.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension m, equipped with the metric g, whose Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by zero. We derive a localized version of Hamilton's gradient estimate for the solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation, which have a positive, smooth, and bounded u. The equation u_t equals the sum of the Laplacian of u and f(u) times the exponential of (p times the negation of u plus (1+p) times the negation of the integral of s times the divergence of the gradient of s over s) is given, where the function f is the given, with the first integral I(s) representing a function. Our findings extend previous works of Souplet and Zhang, Wu and Zhou, and Li and Zhang.

Radio sources detected at low flux densities are difficult to study individually due to limited observational resources.  We employed a novel stacking technique to analyze the average properties of these sources, focusing on those identified by the LOFAR Bright Source Survey within a 1.4 Jy/$\rm deg^{-2}$ source overdensity field.  By examining the characteristics of these sources, we found that angular size alone is insufficient to distinguish between different source types.  Instead, we discovered that compact sources with higher frequency core-like features and fractional core flux densities tend to be blazar-like in nature, whereas those with extended sources and lower fractional core flux densities are more likely to be FR I or lobe-dominated AGN.  This finding suggests that the structural properties of compact radio sources can be effectively characterized by combining angular size with other properties.

This paper introduces abstract hidden Markov models, a new class of systems that model information leakage in probabilistic systems. These models are essentially probability-enhanced hidden Markov models, which incorporate a monadic interface to describe the relationship between observable system actions and the internal states they may be in. By taking an operational approach, we define the semantics of basic building blocks, which then allows us to extend this to more complex systems using a monadic framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a certain type of information leakage, known as bisimilarity, serves as the most detailed probabilistic system comparison standard, which also enables us to define a probabilistic version of effect-free systems and establish a framework for analyzing information leakage in complex systems.

In systems with inherent unpredictability, predictable patterns can emerge due to the interplay between the system's local and non-local properties. This study focuses on understanding the properties of coherent patterns that arise in systems with predictable behavior. We show that a system's inherent unpredictability is reduced to a more manageable level by considering the system's local properties, but the presence of coherent patterns introduces a new type of non-locality. This study reveals that the system's non-local properties are not merely a temporary phenomenon but rather a fundamental characteristic of coherent patterns. Moreover, we found that the system's non-local properties can be quantified in terms of a new measure of distance. This measure of non-locality is found to be related to a system's memory of its past states, and we found that coherent patterns can serve as a new type of non-local resource. This study provides new insights into the relationship between the system's local and non-local properties and suggests that coherent patterns may play a crucial role in understanding the system's overall behavior.
We examine the experimental and theoretical results of scalar E-E' transfers in the region of fast electron scattering, focusing on understanding and predicting this phenomenon.

This paper examines the impact of Casimir effect on blackbody radiation in two environments: a parallel plate and a spherical shell. We consider an idealized perfect blackbody in close proximity to these surfaces and calculate the resulting energy and pressure changes due to thermal fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that the Casimir effect significantly influences blackbody radiation thermodynamics under both configurations, thereby validating the potential for studying quantum effects in systems of large scale.

Protecting users' location privacy is crucial when using location-sensitive mobile devices. This paper focuses on modeling the release of users' locations over time as a sequence of locations, which is a continuous process. Our research examines how a single user's locations can be tracked and predicts their future movements based on past data. To quantify the privacy risk, we use an advanced concept called conditional prior, which measures how much a user's current location can be inferred from their location history. This metric is based on Kullback-Leibler divergence and considers the user's movement as a continuous process. Our analysis reveals that tracking a user's location on a grid increases their privacy risk, but not following a straight path. To address this issue, we developed strategies to minimize the user's location entropy and maintain their privacy by selecting specific paths with grid points.

The <think> operator, used in the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) framework, has been the standard for 3D point cloud-based robotic localization. This has been the case since the early 2000s. The previous implementations of the NDT approach, however, were limited to smaller datasets due to the computational complexity of the 3D operator. This paper presents a new method, based on the Spectral Transformer (ST), to efficiently compute the maximum likelihood estimate for NDT-based localization tasks. The proposed method, called NDT-Transformer, significantly increases the scale of real-world localization datasets, surpassing the current state-of-the-art.

The assessment of functional brain connectivity in multiple sites using resting-state fMRI has been proven to be a valuable research tool, despite concerns about the reproducibility of connectivity measures across multiple sites. Our comprehensive study utilized the 1000 Faces dataset to investigate the reliability and predictive accuracy of resting-state fMRI connectivity across 8 sites, employing an optimized analysis pipeline and various clustering methods. Our results revealed that the reliability of clustering measures varied significantly across multiple sites. Furthermore, we observed that the average within-cluster and between-cluster connectivity measures were more accurate in distinguishing subjects, although the optimal number of clusters varied across multiple sites. Our findings suggest that subject-specific connectivity profiles can be developed to accurately classify subjects, with the number of clusters required varying by site. Our study highlights the need for a more unified approach to clustering analysis and the use of large datasets to improve the reliability and predictive accuracy of connectivity measures across multiple sites.

In a single-hop beeping network, nodes communicate by emitting and listening to signals, with communication occurring when a sending node transmits to a listening neighbor who hears '0' or '1' based on the number of bits transmitted. We investigate energy-efficient naming in this context, where the goal is to minimize total transmission energy while ensuring each node uniquely hears the transmission of every other node using a naming scheme. We demonstrate that a specific class of naming schemes can achieve at most one-fourth of the minimum possible total transmission energy and present a specific example where this energy cost is exactly one-fourth of the minimum possible total transmission energy when the number of nodes is a power of two.

Recent research has demonstrated the potential of pre-trained language models (PLMs) in handling code-mixed text, a form of language that seamlessly integrates two languages in a single utterance. Building upon a novel switching point-based model called SPECTO, designed specifically for detecting language switching points in such text, this paper presents a relative positional encoding technique to enhance SPECTO's effectiveness. Utilizing SPECTO with relative positional encoding yields state-of-the-art results on two major benchmarks: XQuAD and TeluguEnglish XLIST, with relative positional encoding consistently yielding a performance boost.

Using a combination of density functional theory and the more advanced LDA+U and DFT+U methods, we've investigated the electronic and structural properties of H 3 S hydride superconductor across a range of pressures. We found that the material undergoes a significant phase transition near 200 GPa, shifting from a monoclinic C2/m phase to a cubic Pm-3m phase. We then used a combination of density functional theory and the more advanced LDA+U and DFT+U methods to map the van Hove singularities of the material's electronic structure at various pressures. We found that the monoclinic H 3 S material exhibits a strong correlation with its Fermi level near the upper van Hove singularity at approximately 200 GPa. In contrast, the cubic H 3 S material exhibits a similar situation, but with the upper van Hove singularity located at a lower energy. We found that this phenomenon is associated with a significant drop in the material's critical temperature at the phase transition point. We also observed that the material's isotope effect parameter μ is significantly higher in the monoclinic H 3 S material compared to its cubic counterpart, indicating a stronger dependence of the material's critical temperature on isotope substitution. We found that this phenomenon is associated with a stronger coupling between the material's electrons and phonons in the vicinity of the upper van Hove singularity. This paper introduces an innovative method to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic settings. Our approach generates a spatial representation of areas that are safe from collisions, which can be utilized by motion planning algorithms. The proposed technique is implemented within the RRT* path planning algorithm. In dynamic environments, the RRT* algorithm is initially employed to compute a path, which is then utilized to optimize the planning process by restricting search within the identified safe spaces. This paper examines the impact of this strategy on the speed and quality of the resulting paths. Our findings suggest that this RRT*-based technique produces high-quality paths comparable to those generated by the original algorithm, while significantly reducing the time required to compute the path by a factor of up to 40.

This research introduces a visual relocalization technique utilizing 3D surfel maps created from place recognition and 3D reconstruction methods. 3D reconstruction is a challenging process, and map creation is particularly difficult due to the complexity of the estimation and optimization involved. In contrast, surfels prove to be an effective representation, as they strike a balance between visual detail and computational efficiency. In this research, a novel surfel model is proposed, where each surfel is assigned a vector-surfel feature descriptor, learned from data. These features are then used to match 2D image features to map surfels, allowing for camera relocalization. The presented method achieves this by combining image features with geometric constraints in an optimization framework. The project's implementation is available online at https://github.com/alexfeng1994/3D-map-surfel-relocalization.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be cast as a group LASSO problem. By leveraging the sparsity of the precoding vectors, the authors introduce two algorithms - one with an optimal solution and the cyclic algorithm for lower complexity. The former, cyclic algorithm for enhanced efficiency, utilizes an alternating optimization method to achieve higher performance. Experimental results show the cyclic algorithm performs comparably to the group LASSO method, with significantly reduced complexity.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for specific cases like metric graphs and balanced graphs, we can pinpoint the exact set of generators. It is also important to note that, in some instances, the rational function semifield cannot be generated by a finite set over the tropical semifield.

This note demonstrates that a class of Feller semigroups, including those generated by Brownian motions with absorption, uniformly converges to their Q-processes on any compact subset of the state space. Consequently, the result can be applied to characteristically drift Brownian motions under specific boundary conditions to show uniform convergence to the corresponding process without the boundary condition.

We have developed a finite, type three, one-coble invariant known as the $W$-Witten--Reshetikhin--Turaev form. To establish its closed nature, we employed an infinite, free, type three, one-coble invariant, derived from the Fox--Hatcher cycle.

Our study focuses on the role of spin fluctuations in the superconducting properties of the iron-based superconductor LiFeAs, specifically how they impact the superconducting gap structure and the possibility of nematicity in the material. Experimental results from a single crystal of LiFeAs were analyzed using the extended Hubbard model, and the superconducting gap structure was simulated and compared to the experimental data. The analysis revealed that the superconducting gap structure is influenced by the strength of the coupling between electrons and the spin fluctuations, and that the material exhibits s-wave superconducting gap symmetry. Furthermore, our study found that the material does not exhibit nematicity, and that the phase transition at 17 K is solely a superconducting transition. Our study also found that the LiFeAs compound behaves differently from other iron-based superconductors, such as BaFe2As2, and that the phase transition in LiFeAs occurs at a much lower temperature.

Diverse alignment-agnostic non-Higgs boson constraints from electroweak precision tests, flavor constraints, and dark matter research are also factored in. Projections of dark photon constraints from the future lepton collider are incorporated into the model. Distributions of the Higgs boson masses in the plane of the two Higgs doublet model's parameter space are determined for both aligned and non-aligned models, using the global fit results. The model parameters are translated into the two Higgs doublet model's non-aligned parameter space, and the degree of alignment is quantified.
