This study investigates the problem of distributed control in systems organized on graphs, with an emphasis on maintaining symmetry within the resulting graph-symmetric subsystems. The presented approach utilizes graph filter design to achieve this control objective, with specific instructions on implementing the filters in a distributed manner. The analysis demonstrates that the proposed graph filters can be computed using a variant of the distributed subgradient method, with the convergence rate directly influenced by the network connectivity. The approach is validated through a simulation example in this research.

Image search systems that utilize textual queries are limited by the lack of precise control users have over the query process. In contrast, our interactive image indexing system allows users to refine and adjust the query parameters in real-time, thereby enhancing the relevance of the indexing results. Notably, our approach does not require access to the system backend and can be implemented as a standalone tool. By doing so, it enables researchers to rapidly assess the effectiveness of various metrics for different types of data, such as specific types of images or categories. We conducted an experiment using this system to evaluate the performance of different metrics for identifying subcategories within the Flickr dataset, thereby demonstrating the utility of our solution.

This study explores the possibility of secure communication in a noisy environment using only channel noise for authentication purposes. The investigation centers on distinguishing between two types of transmitted signals - one generated by the legitimate sender and another by an imposter - through statistical analysis of their impact on a receiver's output. The analysis employs the Kullback-Leibler divergence to quantify the distinguishability of these signals and employs the Sanov theorem to evaluate the performance of the sender and sender verification processes. The analysis is conducted for both uncorrelated and autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models of white Gaussian noise and reveals that the sender's error rate is influenced by the length of the transmitted signal and the variance of the noise, while the sender's error rate is determined by the length of the transmitted signal and the order of the noise process. The study also examines the feasibility of extending this communication method to wireless networks and sheds light on the challenges associated with implementing it in such networks.

A theoretical model, based on the concept of dispersionless and position-dependent transport, has been developed to investigate energy transport in systems of nonhomogeneous driven elements. In this model, the effects of dispersion are considered to be negligible, and a local analysis reveals that the driving force is the sole determinant of directed motion. Consequently, the steady-state velocity of energy transport and the associated current are expressed as functions of the driving force and a potential landscape. This model accurately describes and replicates the experimentally observed patterns of directed transport and wave propagation in nonhomogeneous resistively shunted Josephson junction arrays. Furthermore, the model accurately accounts for the experimentally measured transport characteristics of junction arrays with a sinusoidal resistive landscape and offers a framework for understanding dispersionless and directed transport in nonhomogeneous resistive networks.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to locally projecting impulse responses, allowing for more adaptable estimation by using a data-driven adjustment of the smoothing span. Our technique, grounded in Bayesian kernel smoothing, enhances traditional methods and mitigates potential biases, particularly those stemming from event overlap in impulse response analysis. By incorporating a precise evaluation of asymptotic properties, we develop flexible estimation with a consistently reliable small-sample benchmark. Our innovation is further validated through integration with the Dynamic Local Projection package, exemplified by a detailed examination of U.S. monetary policy impact on output and inflation.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge $q$ moving in a uniform magnetic field. This scenario, known as the Hall effect, causes the vacuum to produce angular momentum due to $q$ interacting with the electromagnetic field's zero-point fluctuations. As $q$ moves in the presence of an external field, it also disturbs the vacuum, resulting in a non-zero angular Casimir momentum that opposes the direction of $q$'s motion. This phenomenon is analogous to a frictional force opposing motion and arises from the vacuum's response to $q$'s movement. Notably, the vacuum's influence on angular momentum is distinct from its effect on energy, where it causes energy shifts in $q$'s motion but does not alter its average angular momentum.

The traditional fine-grained named entity typing task is hampered by limited training data and the difficulty of defining entity categories a priori. To address this challenge, we introduce FGNET-RH, a novel framework that leverages hyperbolic geometry to encode hierarchical entity types and mitigate data scarcity. By transforming the target labels into a space of non-negative integers, FGNET-RH eliminates the need for pre-defined category sets. Our method excels on three challenging FG-NET datasets under both joint and incremental learning scenarios. Our implementation is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/lyu-yuanyuan/FGNET-RH.

This paper establishes upper limits on the second Hankel determinant for functions within the class U, providing precise validation of past conjectures proposed by Alebachew. Furthermore, similar determinative proofs are offered for the second Hankel determinant in relation to the general class S, specifically yielding sharp estimates for $H_{2,3}(f)$ with confirmed Conjecture 1.2.

Achieving efficient resource utilization in cloud computing virtualization requires load balancing across servers. However, overcommitment of resources in virtual machines can lead to unequal server loads, hindering the load balancing process. To address this issue, we introduce Prepartition, a novel virtual machine partitioning algorithm that dynamically adjusts the resources allocated to each VM to balance loads among servers. Our approach, along with an associated resource allocation scheme, ensures that each server is fully utilized, promoting efficient resource utilization. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Prepartition in balancing loads among servers.

In game theory, characterizing outcomes through equilibrium concepts such as Nash equilibrium is crucial, but predicting equilibria in complex games is complicated by the challenges of generating and representing game structures, as well as the existence of multiple equilibria. To address these issues, the new approach employs Fixed Point Networks (FPNs) to directly model the endogenous nature of equilibrium outcomes, eliminating the need for game structure representation. By utilizing neural networks that converge to a fixed point, the method achieves robust performance in predicting diverse equilibrium types across multiple game families. Additionally, the approach demonstrates the ability to generalize to novel, unseen games.

In non-experimental settings, we can derive strict limitations on causal effects by leveraging causal diagrams and bounds on the variables in the study. By incorporating functional forms, we can tighten these limits and apply them to observational data. The developed approach enables us to handle high-dimensional data, allowing for an assessment of the proximity of any causal effect to its lower or upper bounds through a connection with compressed sensing. The validity of this method is illustrated through simulations, demonstrating that causal effects can sometimes be estimated with greater accuracy than even highly informative surrogate outcomes.

This study focuses on online monitoring of systems affected by covert cyber attacks, focusing on systems that are linear, autonomous, and operate in closed environments. At each time step, the sensor values from the system are compared to expected readings using a pre-established threshold. If the sensor values deviate significantly, the monitoring system signals a potential attack. Previous studies have proposed monitoring methods for systems with attack-free assumptions, but these approaches are limited by their reliance on real-time measurements, which can be compromised during attacks, and their inability to generalize across various attack scenarios. This study develops a predictive monitoring approach specifically designed for systems that are subject to covert attacks. By analyzing past sensor data, the proposed method can predict future system behavior and compare it to expected outcomes, thereby detecting attacks. This approach is validated through simulations of an 8-dimensional autonomous vehicle system, which demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting stealthy attacks.

A groundbreaking approach called GAE-ISumm is introduced, which utilizes an unsupervised deep learning model to extract the most significant sentences from lengthy documents by condensing them into concise summaries. By leveraging a deep auto-encoder architecture, this method employs a graph-based representation of sentences to differentiate meaningful from the less significant ones. To achieve this, a novel embedding technique called SUME is developed, which incorporates a sentence's semantic content and its position within the document, thereby enhancing the accuracy of sentence importance prediction. Evaluations across multiple Indian languages have demonstrated that GAE-ISumm surpasses the GEA model, utilizing a deep auto-encoder architecture, thereby validating the efficacy of SUME.

A commutative s-ring of functions, defined on an infinite set of arbitrary nature, is referred to as being of Krull type if it adheres to specific criteria outlined in this study. These conditions establish that the s-ring comprises all functions mapping a group to its integral closure of zero, specifically to $\mathbb{I}(G)$. Furthermore, the structure of such s-rings is characterized as being isomorphic to the direct sum of s-rings consisting of functions with bounded range in each component of the primary components of $G$.

The peculiar motion of a few stars has been observed in the local universe, 
which can be partially attributed to the gravitational influence of an unseen object. 
A recent study has examined the movement of a particular group of rapidly changing stars, 
which exhibit a distinct pattern in the northern sky. This pattern is believed to be 
caused by the presence of a massive, unseen companion orbiting these stars. 
Researchers have analyzed data from the Gaia mission and found evidence of the 
gravitational influence of these companions, which have been found to have masses 
ranging from 0.1 to 10 times the mass of the sun. 
A statistical analysis has been performed to determine the likelihood of the 
companion's existence and to estimate its mass and separation from the star. 
The results of this study have implications for the search for dark matter and 
for the understanding of the formation of binary star systems.

Deep learning models, particularly those based on variational autoencoders, have gained significant attention in various applications. The traditional variational autoencoder employs probabilistic modeling, utilizing maximum likelihood estimation to capture latent variable distributions. In this paper, we introduce a new regularization approach to the least square variational autoencoder, aiming to derive a closed-form solution for the optimal network weights. The proposed solution leverages a minimum eigenvalue constraint, ensuring that the network's kernel matrix remains positive semi-definite, thus enabling efficient parameter estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the equivalence of our proposed minimum eigenvalue constraint to the traditional 1/λ constraint commonly applied in inverse eigenvalue problems, highlighting its versatility and adaptability.

Smart home technology has become a significant part of people's lives, providing convenience and comfort. However, the risk of cyber threats and data breaches is a serious concern, posing potential harm to individuals' lives and property.  This study aims to address these security risks by developing an IoT-based smart home monitoring system, incorporating private blockchain and wireless localization technologies to safeguard users' data and prevent malicious attacks.  A private blockchain network is established, enabling the verification of each IoT device's legitimacy and the monitoring of their activities.  Additionally, the proposed system employs wireless localization to safeguard the home's physical security by detecting unauthorized access and triggering a blockchain transaction.  A prototype of the proposed system has been successfully implemented and tested, with promising results.

A novel approach for generating gray-coded phase and quadrature components from a L-value in a software-defined radio decoder has been developed. This innovative method employs a deep learning-based technique, specifically utilizing a convolutional neural network, to achieve the goal. The proposed method was tested on various L-value ranges and with different neural networks, including U-Nets, and demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods, especially in low L-value scenarios. The experimental results revealed that the new method reduced bit errors when using differential modulation and offered improved overall performance.

We have developed two parameterized algorithms for determining the up-down connectivity of acyclic graphs, focusing on specific structural components. The first algorithm has a runtime of $O(2^{2\textsc{Tw}}\cdot n^2)$, where $\textsc{Tw}$ represents the maximum vertex degree sum, and it leverages the components' trees. The second algorithm, designed to process cyclic structures, runs in $O(2^{2\textsc{C}}\cdot n^2)$ time, with $\textsc{C}$ representing the size of these components, and it can also identify a planar embedding for graphs that can be drawn upwards. The complexity of our algorithms is influenced by the choice of parameterized component size, and we have established a relationship between this parameter and the size of the minimum vertex cover in certain graph classes.

The rapid growth of data from crowdsourced studies and community-driven initiatives presents a dual-edged sword for the machine learning community. On one hand, it enables the development of more realistic models and increased model transparency through the utilization of more realistic data. On the other hand, it poses significant challenges due to the unstructured and noisy nature of these datasets. In this research, we introduce an innovative approach to tackle the difficulties associated with these datasets by leveraging the strengths of ensemble modeling, human-generated uncertainty distributions, and entropy-based measures. Our proposed approach involves combining multiple models to mitigate the effects of data noise and utilizes uncertainty distributions to quantify the level of uncertainty in human-generated data. Our results demonstrate that this approach can significantly improve the accuracy of machine learning models and increase their interpretability, making them more reliable tools for understanding human behavior and decision-making processes.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, we derive bounds on the operator norms of Ruelle-Thermodynamic transfer operators in various function spaces. These bounds are applied to analyze the rate of operator norm decay for additive cocycles in dynamical systems.

A particular form of multi-dimensional data called a covering array is used to create efficient test suites that can detect certain types of errors. The number of symbols in these arrays can be minimized, and a formula has been developed to estimate the minimum number of symbols for a given level of interaction and error detection capability. The minimum number of symbols is denoted by the function $\text{ACA}(r,N,S)$, which represents the minimum number of symbols in a covering array with $r$ levels of interaction and size $N$. The function $\text{ACA}(r,N,2)$ is particularly useful for testing software, as it can identify errors that occur when two symbols interact incorrectly. The function $\text{ACA}(r,N,3)$ is less useful for testing purposes, as it requires more test cases to detect errors that occur when three symbols interact incorrectly. The paper focuses on the properties of $\text{ACA}(r,N,2)$ and uses them to develop the first non-recursive construction for arrays with two symbols, which can reduce the number of symbols in test suites. The construction is based on the concept of difference families, and it is used to develop a new family of test suites that can detect errors that occur when two symbols interact incorrectly.

A nonlocal game is a two-player contest involving shared randomness, where Mary and Charlie collaborate to achieve optimal success rates, despite the effects of nonlocality. Nonlocal strategies, which can't be replicated classically, are achieved through quantum entanglement. This paper focuses on games played with noisy maximally entangled states, which can be thought of as slightly imperfect versions of perfectly entangled states. We demonstrate that determining whether a quantum strategy exists for such games remains a solvable problem, even for states with significant errors. This breakthrough relies on a key finding that checking specific types of matrices for positive definiteness makes the problem easier. Our result has significant implications for understanding the limitations of certain types of strategies, including those used in data-hiding protocols.

This study aims to assess the performance of the Guided Genetic Algorithm (GGA) proposed by Alshammari et al. in automating the crash reproduction process. Our objective is to verify the GGA's effectiveness by analyzing its results on a test case, specifically the YouTube video "Windows 10 is TERRIBLE!" which features a highly entertaining and complex scenario. Given the GGA's reliance on visual elements, we focused on integrating its navigational and content-based features into our evaluation. Upon implementing the GGA, we encountered difficulties in replicating the content-based feature due to the presence of text in the video. Consequently, we concentrated on analyzing the navigational feature and discovered that it achieved a coverage of 70% of the video's navigational steps. Although the results demonstrate promising coverage, further investigation is required to enhance the GGA's performance and increase step coverage in the video.

Researchers have used thermal photons to study the properties of the quark-gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions. They have found that the anisotropic flow of these photons can serve as a sensitive indicator of the plasma's viscosity. By applying a novel technique, the team has calculated the elliptic flow of photons for different centralities of gold-gold collisions at a specific energy. Comparing these results with experimental data has revealed that the plasma has lower viscosity than predicted, which is consistent with previous measurements. Furthermore, the team has discovered that the anisotropic flow of photons is more sensitive to the plasma's properties than other particles. This finding suggests that photons can provide valuable insights into the early stages of heavy-ion collisions.

Building on the kagome lattice, we derive its K and HgCl2 sub-lattices, finding key three-spin interactions for kagome and kagome-honeycomb systems, which facilitate the transition to regular magnetic patterns. We employ the classical Heisenberg model to analyze regular magnetic orders in kagome and kagome-honeycomb lattices with long-range exchange, and predict their temperature-dependent spin fluctuations using the spin-wave method. Our findings suggest that kagome-honeycomb lattices with long-range exchange exhibit enhanced spin fluctuations and reduced ordering temperatures compared to square-honeycomb lattices with the same exchange range.

Large-scale data analysis often involves analyzing multiple tests simultaneously, 
resulting in a need for new statistical methods that can handle the dependencies between tests. 
In the context of large-scale data analysis, identifying causal relationships is crucial, 
but traditional methods may not be effective when dealing with dependent tests. 
To address this challenge, a new method called Treatment Effect Detection with Controlled False Discovery Rate (TEDR) has been proposed. 
TEDR uses a novel statistic called the Zin-statistic, which can handle dependent tests, 
and incorporates a False Discovery Rate controlling procedure based on the Benjamini-Hochberg method. 
To demonstrate the effectiveness of TEDR, it was applied to the analysis of gene expression data from a large-scale study. 
The results showed that TEDR was able to control the False Discovery Rate while identifying significant treatment effects. 
To further validate TEDR, it was compared to other existing methods, such as the Benjamini-Hochberg and Storey's methods. 
The results of the analysis showed that TEDR was able to outperform the other methods in terms of its ability to identify significant treatment effects. 
In conclusion, TEDR represents a novel approach to large-scale data analysis that can handle dependent tests, 
and has been shown to be effective in the analysis of gene expression data.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, the conditions for its stabilization, and the mechanism for universe reheating are outlined. The inflation theory's connection to the observation of cosmic microwave background radiation temperature fluctuations is also discussed.

The CDF II collaboration's $W$ boson mass measurement deviates from the Standard Model prediction by $7.0\sigma$. We find the compatibility of $W$ boson mass and the anomalous magnetic moment of muons within the Type-X two Higgs doublet model. Introducing a non-zero $\delta\sin\beta$ can resolve the conflict between the two anomalies in this model. The conflict can be resolved in the Type-X 2HDM with $\delta\sin\beta\simeq 0.01$ for tan $\beta$ $\simeq$ 10.

Software developers often struggle to find specific concepts within large codebases due to inconsistent renaming and vague search queries. To address this issue, we investigated using crowd-sourced knowledge to improve automatic reformulation of search queries. Our approach combines crowd-sourced knowledge with query reformulation techniques to locate relevant code concepts more accurately. We proposed and tested a novel query reformulation technique called QUICKAR, which leverages crowd-sourced knowledge to identify and utilize contextual relationships between search terms and target concepts. Our experiments demonstrated that our solution significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art query reformulation techniques, achieving a mean average precision of 0.45 compared to the best available methods.

Adaptive adjustment of prosodic elements in real-time during dialogue is known as entrainment and occurs across various domains, including clinical settings and everyday conversations. The phenomenon of automatic adaptation of speech rate is a well-documented case of entrainment. Despite its significance, research on detecting entrainment remains limited. This study proposes a deep neural network approach to identify and quantify automatic adaptation of speech rate. The proposed method involves using dynamic neural networks to estimate and compare conditional distributions of speech rate in speakers' utterances, based on the duration of preceding utterances. Experimental results using a large dataset of spontaneous conversations demonstrate the effectiveness of neural models in identifying and quantifying automatic adaptation of speech rate, and show that learned neural models outperform traditional statistical models in this task.

We have developed an open-source visualization tool, RCSEDv2, to streamline the analysis of data collected from radio telescopes, combining imaging and spectral analysis capabilities within a web-based environment. This platform incorporates advanced radio data visualization and analysis tools, enabling the examination of complex data formats, such as the MSK7 format, through data visualization and analysis features, including imaging, spectral analysis, and the detection of point sources. Furthermore, RCSEDv2 includes collaborative web tools for the analysis of radio telescope data, including the comparison of different data sets and the integration of external catalog information. The underlying visualization and analysis libraries, RCViz and RSpec, are also available for standalone use, providing additional functionality for the community to leverage in their own projects.

Temporal action segmentation is a complex task that requires accurately identifying the onset and end of actions within continuous video streams. A major challenge in doing so is the lack of labeled data, which hinders the development of effective segmentation methods. To address this issue, a new approach called Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP) is proposed. SSCAP leverages self-supervised learning to identify and group similar actions, allowing for more accurate segmentation. SSCAP consists of two main components: a framework for unsupervised temporal action parsing and a refinement module that leverages the established parsing to improve refined parsed actions. SSCAP achieves a high level of accuracy on several benchmark datasets, including DUD, X-VIGGO, and VIGGO, and also demonstrates accurate human-aligned parsed actions.

We have discovered that a class of hadronic molecular states, consisting of baryon-meson pairs, can be formed through the recombination process driven by a specific current, and our analysis shows that this mechanism is highly effective in generating states, such as the $P_{c}(3055)$. Furthermore, we have found that this recombination mechanism is also responsible for the production of these states in $\bar{p}p$ collisions, and it is a natural outcome of the chiral unitary approach. Additionally, we have demonstrated that the production rates of the $P_{c}(3055)$ and $P_{c}(3100)$ states are comparable to those of their non-resonant counterparts, and their production mechanism is quite natural. Moreover, we have shown that the $P_{c}(3055)$ state can be identified through a distinct angular distribution in the $\Sigma_{c}\bar{\pi}$ system and that its properties can be measured by analyzing the angular distribution in the $\Xi_{c}\bar{K}$ system. Furthermore, we have found that the $P_{c}(3055)$ state can decay into $\Sigma_{c}\bar{\pi}$ and $J/\psi p$ channels through the exchange of light mesons, and its decay width into the $J/\psi p$ channel is relatively small, and it is also possible to observe this decay in $\bar{p}

In computer science education, particularly in software engineering, effective feedback is a crucial factor for student success. Current software engineering education often relies on traditional code review and detailed feedback methods, but these may not be the most effective. A novel approach called Inquiry-Based Conceptual Feedback (IBCF) has been developed to promote conceptual understanding through a question-and-answer format. A study involving 120 students compared the efficacy of IBCF against two traditional feedback methods: detailed feedback from peers and instructors. The results showed that IBCF led to a significant increase in student performance, with those who received this type of feedback scoring an average of 73.5% on a post-test, compared to 58.3% for detailed feedback from peers and 64.3% for detailed feedback from instructors. This research provides empirical evidence that IBCF is a more effective feedback mechanism in software engineering education.

Domain adaptation is a common machine learning challenge that occurs when there's a discrepancy between the data distributions of a training model and its target environment. This phenomenon is particularly significant in real-world applications, where the ideal scenario of collecting a vast amount of labeled data from the target domain is often impractical. Domain experts typically have access to data from the target domain, but labeling it is costly. To address this issue, semi-supervised domain adaptation has been developed, which involves adapting a pre-trained model with limited labels from the target domain. However, the effectiveness of these methods is often hindered by the scarcity of labels, which can lead to suboptimal results. To overcome this limitation, we propose a cost-effective approach called Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Transfer (S2Ht), which utilizes class predictions from target data to augment the training set and improve the pre-trained model. By iteratively adapting the model with both original and predicted data, S2Ht achieves substantial improvements in adaptation accuracy, particularly in challenging scenarios.

A novel nuclear propulsion system, characterized by a gas core reactor, is proposed for deep space exploration and interplanetary travel. In this design, the working fluid is a nuclear fuel in gaseous form, which is magnetically confined and circulated through a propulsion system. The resulting thermal energy is transferred to a surrounding propellant, which is then expelled at high velocity. A numerical analysis of this concept was conducted, which involved solving the magnetohydrodynamics equations for the plasma and a separate energy equation for the non-magnetically confined surrounding fluid. By utilizing an existing correlation for nucleate boiling in helium, the thermal energy transfer between the plasma and the surrounding fluid was determined. This transfer was analyzed in terms of the pressure and the geometry of the propulsion system.

Developing neural networks to accurately identify the precise area where neutrino-charged particle interactions occur within large-scale astroparticle research facilities. Unlike traditional methods, these networks learn the underlying physical laws governing these interactions, enhancing their ability to localize events. We utilize multiple Monte Carlo simulations to train the networks, incorporating both the research facility's simulated data and additional research from the Particle Data Group. The results show that these networks successfully achieve a high level of accuracy, comparable to or surpassing conventional algorithms. Furthermore, incorporating external information about the research facility's underlying physics significantly boosts the network's performance.

The study of substellar objects and giant exoplanet atmospheres involves analyzing their infrared spectra through photometry and spectroscopy. However, interpreting these observations requires accurate, up-to-date information on molecular absorption properties. Existing databases for key molecules such as H2O, CH4, and CO are incomplete and often lack coverage of important parameters like temperature, pressure, and self-broadening effects. As a result, researchers often rely on the HITRAN database, despite its limitations for these specific conditions. To address these shortcomings, EXOPLINES has been developed, providing a comprehensive collection of absorption cross-sections for key molecules found in atmospheric spectra of substellar objects and hot exoplanets. The database, covering temperatures from 50 to 3000 K and including detailed data on line shapes and broadening coefficients, can be accessed online or through command-line interface, facilitating accurate atmospheric characterization and enabling precise comparisons with observations.

This study investigates the underlying principles of grounding in Answer Set Programming, specifically focusing on the processing time and memory requirements for grounding disjunctions in logic programs. We examine three key factors: the use of stable models, the use of answer sets, and the use of partial answer sets. By analyzing these approaches, we aim to clarify the time and space complexities associated with grounding in this context.

Quantum resource theories identify specific properties of individual systems or collections of systems that enable the assignment of value to states within a given framework. The state space within these theories is characterized by free states, which lack resource content, and non-free states, which possess some form of resource. The relative cost of transforming one state into another is determined by the monotonous properties that characterize the inherent value of the states. The cost function is defined as the minimum required amount of a resource to execute a task, which is the fundamental quantity of interest in this study. The results of this investigation show that the cost function adheres to a first law, which states that the total change in cost function values across a state evolution equals the total external resource input plus the total work done on the state. The study further reveals that this first law can be modified to an inequality in the presence of uncontrolled, freely available resources. The research demonstrates the applicability of this inequality to two prominent examples: the coherence theory and the entanglement theory. The research also provides a method for quantifying the work that can be extracted from a state when an arbitrary amount of resource is provided, which is the total work minus the cost function value. The study shows that this extractable work is equivalent to the total work that must be input to execute the inverse task. The results of this investigation are further illustrated by the example of state transformations in coherence theory, which are achieved using the relative entropy of incoherence as a resource

To quantify information derived from random variables, we introduce a general measure $\mathcal{I}_\mathcal{F}(X)$, which is defined by a set of central moments $\mathcal{F}(X)$. The measure $\mathcal{I}_\mathcal{F}(X)$ is given by the number of possible functions $f$ that are zeroth through the order of the highest moment in $\mathcal{F}(X)$, such that the expected value of each $f$ differs from its expected value under the uniform distribution. The measure captures a range of information entropy measures, including the uniform distribution and the Gaussian distribution. The measure $\mathcal{I}_\mathcal{F}(X)$ also enables the investigation of unique properties, including non-decreasing behavior, the absence of memory, and the lack of scalability.

We investigate the temporal evolution of high-dimensional multivariate time series with heavy-tailed properties. In contrast to traditional time series models, we establish nonparametric invariants that remain unchanged over time and develop their associated asymptotic distribution theory. Building on this foundation, we establish the convergence rate of kernel estimators for invariants and create data-driven diagnostic tools to evaluate model fit. Finally, we propose a novel method for forecasting future multivariate time series data based on heavy-tailed non-stationary characteristics.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, offering a robust solution for quantum error correction. These codes combine strong error-control capabilities with efficient decoding algorithms, enabling a trade-off between rate and distance. The rate of these codes approaches a non-zero limit as their distance increases, while their distance scales with a power of the distance parameter. A significant aspect of these codes lies in their ability to be decoded in linear time, achieved through a combination of check node messages and message passing algorithms. A recent refinement, called X check node messages, improves the decoding process by reducing the computational complexity. Furthermore, simulations indicate that these codes exhibit enhanced performance when subjected to various quantum noise conditions, including depolarizing noise, outperforming alternative codes. A comprehensive analysis of the codes' performance is also provided, incorporating analytical approximations and Monte Carlo simulations.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem in graphs involves finding a subset of vertices $V'$, such that every vertex in the graph is within a distance of $r$ from a vertex in $V'$. This corresponds to finding an independent dominating set in the $r$-power of the graph, denoted as $G^r$. Recent research has shown that this problem is difficult to solve efficiently in various settings, including random graphs and high-girth graphs. We present a new algorithm for high-girth sparse high-degree graphs that runs in randomized distributed time $O(r^2 \log^2 n)$. This algorithm is an improvement over previous results, which showed that the problem is solvable in $O(r^3 \log^2 n)$ time. Our results also imply that the problem is solvable in $O(r^3 \log^3 n)$ time in high-girth graphs with more general properties.

This research examines the impact of disorder on the bulk-boundary correspondence in disordered three-dimensional topological systems. Through numerical studies, we investigate the relationship between bulk and boundary properties, revealing that the bulk-bulk correlation remains intact even under disorder, while the bulk-boundary correspondence breaks down. We explore the consequences of broken bulk-boundary correspondence on boundary states, finding that their localization lengths are influenced by both disorder strength and dimensionality. The results indicate that the boundary states become delocalized above a certain disorder threshold, which is determined by the bulk's disorder threshold. Additionally, we reveal a connection between the breaking of bulk-boundary correspondence and the delocalization of bulk states, providing insight into the broader implications of this phenomenon.

Significant results from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have substantially narrowed down the viable areas of supersymmetric model parameter space. This paper delves into new research on gluino and squark decays, specifically examining three types of final states: b-quark pairs, leptons and photons, and missing transverse momentum. Our analysis focuses on gluino decays into b-quarks and leptons/photons facilitated by Z or γ states, as well as squark pair production resulting in b-quark and missing transverse momentum outcomes. Notably, this analysis relies on simulated gluino and squark decays rather than assuming stable neutralinos. With an integrated luminosity of 35 inverse femtobarns, our search sets stringent 95% confidence level limits on gluino masses up to 1.2 TeV in various LHC models, and squark masses as low as 600 GeV in several models.

We introduce a novel, flexible system for light field rendering, which can be further customized using learned rendering functions. Our system combines an efficient volume rendering approach, high-order light field decomposition, and depth-based segmentation to produce high-quality light field views from multiple z-layers. Our depth-segmentation technique, utilizing voxelized point clouds, enables the accurate extraction of multiple objects and significantly improves segmentation results. Our system's versatility is demonstrated through successful applications in standard datasets, real-time light field view synthesis, and neural light field decompression.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020, utilizing the SCIAMMY interferometer, yielded 48 successful datasets out of 51 attempts. These observations covered 37 binary systems, with 12 systems observed for the first time and the remaining systems observed multiple times. Notably, 11 new orbital solutions were derived from the collected data. Additionally, the study of binary stars' rotation through orbital configuration analysis proved successful for 14 stars, and the study of planetary systems' stellar companions was established for two stars. Furthermore, the study of binary systems with known exoplanets was established for four stars. A comprehensive analysis of binary properties, including their mass ratios, revealed that the distribution of mass ratios at the observed orbital phases aligns with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the study of binary systems' properties at the observed orbital phases showed that their mass ratios were in line with theoretical predictions. Additionally, the study of binary systems with known mass ratios revealed that their mass ratios were in line with theoretical predictions.

We are investigating chiral celestial algebras, a concept that encompasses chiral algebras of celestial conformal field theory, to explore their structure and make progress in understanding the associated celestial CFT. By extending the chiral algebra framework to more general symmetry algebras, we find that certain conditions are required for the chiral symmetry to emerge, a scenario that is exemplified by the SU(N) Yang-Mills theory. A new method to construct these algebras is also developed, a technique that is particularly useful in cases where the symmetry algebras are more complex, such as when the symmetry is U(N) rather than SU(N). We further derive a colour-kinematics duality for the SU(N) and U(N) Yang-Mills theories, a phenomenon that is rooted in the properties of the celestial algebra. We also explore the structure of the celestial OPE for SU(N) and U(N) Yang-Mills theory and find that it is composed of a sum over soft and hard gluon operators, a result that is derived from the properties of the Lie algebra. We demonstrate that certain terms in the celestial OPE are integrable and can be expressed as a sum over lower-dimensional operators, a result that is particularly useful in the context of the SU(N) and U(N) Yang-Mills theories.

A powerful solar eruption, specifically a binary filament ejection accompanied by a coronal mass ejection, was analyzed using multiple image and spectral data sets collected via the 150 MHz Low Frequency Array. The data revealed a shock wave moving at approximately 1000 km/s in the lower corona, significantly faster than expected in the solar atmosphere. This shock wave was observed to be driven by a narrow jet emanating from an active region, providing a unique opportunity to study the effects of jet-piston shock interactions in the low corona. The analysis revealed discrepancies between the observed shock speed and theoretical models, suggesting that current models may be inadequate for predicting shock behavior in this environment.

A comprehensive likelihood analysis is performed on the general two Higgs doublet model, taking into account the current anomalies observed in lepton flavour physics and the recent experimental results. Furthermore, the model's predictive capabilities for the muon anomalous magnetic moment and its cousin, the smau, are evaluated. The model's parameter space is thoroughly constrained using a combination of Higgs physics and non-Higgs physics benchmarks, such as $B\to \mu\mu$ decays, double Higgs production, and direct search bounds. The parameter space is divided into three distinct regions based on the lepton universal coupling scale $\Lambda$, with each region characterized by distinct phenomenological properties. Notably, Region 1 is consistent with the current anomalies and agrees with the smau prediction, while Regions 2 and 3 exhibit smau predictions that are in conflict with the measured value.

This work introduces a new approach to modeling the dynamic behavior of random, two-dimensional vectors that undergo continuous changes. Building upon the work of Hairer and Mattingly in their study of Markov semigroups for functional differential equations, we leverage their findings to provide a existence and uniqueness proof for the solution functional differential equations in a functional setting. We further demonstrate how this solution can be used to establish the Markov property of the resulting process and obtain an associated functional semigroup. We also show through a specific example that the solution can explicitly be represented by functional distributions in the case of linear functional stochastic differential equations.

Utilizing quantum simulation, we examine the state vector of the system at m output modes, where the state's entanglement is quantified by the von Neumann entropy. Our results show that the entanglement reaches its maximum when the state is projected onto m modes with mode numbers half the total, given n modes and n photons. Interestingly, the entanglement reaches its minimum value when m modes exhibit no overlap with the input state, such as n modes with mode numbers half the total plus one, given an even n. Temporal sequence analysis in life science research is a critical challenge, particularly with temporal sequence classification tasks.  The limitations of current methods stem from their reliance on manual feature engineering and the need for lengthy sequences to achieve satisfactory results.  The introduction of deep learning techniques has significantly improved feature extraction and classification, but these methods still struggle with short and diverse sequence lengths.  In response, a new deep learning approach, the Transformer model, has been developed to effectively handle such complexities, especially to analyze short sequences with high-dimensional sequences.  The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated in temporal sequence classification tasks using synthetic and real-life data, including intracellular calcium signals and electrocardiogram signals.  The results show that the Transformer model outperforms other models in these tasks and can accurately classify short and diverse sequences with high-dimensional sequences, thereby providing a new approach to temporal sequence analysis in life science research.

Reinforcement learning has proven effective for making decisions in complex environments, particularly through the use of feedforward neural networks. However, when dealing with uncertain information, these networks often need to make assumptions, which can be problematic. We found that in highly ambiguous situations, agents trained with standard feedforward networks tend to struggle, particularly when adapting to significant changes. We discovered that incorporating recurrent neural networks into the learning process can significantly improve an agent's ability to thrive in highly unpredictable environments. We also identified the critical role of internal state representations in facilitating this success. Furthermore, through the use of information theory, we found that the improvements achieved by recurrent networks are directly linked to their capacity to accurately assess their own understanding of the environment.

In video-based action detection, precise location and classification of actions within long sequences of data are critical challenges. Current approaches often rely on extensive, frame-by-frame action annotations, which are time-consuming and costly to produce. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed weakly-supervised methods that leverage more affordable temporal action localizations. However, these methods still struggle to accurately classify actions, particularly in segments where key features are missing. To address this issue, we propose a graph-based approach that utilizes unlabelled data to enhance action classification accuracy. By representing each frame as a node in the graph and propagating information across related frames, we can effectively combine context and improve action detection performance. Through thorough experimentation on multiple datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in improving action detection accuracy, even with limited weak supervision.

The Image Similarity Challenge 2021, a data science competition, focused on identifying image similarities using three distinct types of datasets: Deforested, Fashion, and CelebA. The datasets were characterized by their unique sampling methods, resulting in imbalanced data distributions. The primary task was to develop models capable of predicting image similarity scores for query and support image pairs, using various real-world and synthetic datasets. Notably, participants were required to submit results on a test set, while a validation set was also provided for additional analysis. This paper presents an overview of the competition, a detailed examination of the submitted models, and an in-depth discussion of the experimental outcomes, model submissions, and the competition's evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the paper delves into the implications of the competition's results for future research in the field of image similarity assessment.

This work explores the long-term behavior of solutions to a parabolic partial differential equation, specifically one with degenerating coefficients, defined within a bounded domain that undergoes periodic changes over time. By examining a family of perturbed versions of this domain, we examine how solutions evolve over time. Our approach involves developing a topological framework to study the convergence of these solutions, taking into account boundary conditions of Dirichlet and Neumann types. This allows us to establish a general theory that encompasses both metastable and homogenization phenomena in stable long-term solutions of parabolic equations. This theory is then applied to two specific cases: analyzing the rate of convergence in the metastable scenario and studying the limiting behavior in the homogenization scenario where fast oscillations occur in a perturbation parameter.

Using the lowest order canonical vertex correction (LOCV) within the relativistic mean-field theory (RMT), the effect of a strong magnetic field on the properties of nuclear matter was investigated. It was found that in the presence of a strong magnetic field, the gap equation and the LOCV integral equation were modified, leading to changes in the nuclear matter energy per nucleon, symmetry energy, and the binding energy of $^{208}$Pb. Furthermore, calculations showed that the gap equation's solution results in asymmetric gaps between positive and negative energy states, implying that particles in the positive energy gap are more stable than those in the negative energy gap.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a significant concern in distributed machine learning. While efficient distributed gradient compression techniques have been developed, they are not compatible with differential privacy, which is essential for protecting data. This research proposes a novel approach that integrates data privacy and communication efficiency by introducing a differentially private quantization method. The proposed algorithm achieves a significant reduction in communication costs while ensuring data privacy, with a quantization complexity of O(log(d)/ε²) for a given level of privacy protection. Furthermore, theoretical analysis confirms that this approach maintains the accuracy required for generalization. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this approach achieves substantial reductions in communication costs, with data privacy guarantees under challenging conditions.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet survey of the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga star complex has been conducted, focusing on the star-forming regions of IC 348, IC 48, and the Lupus clouds. The survey employed the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer to obtain 115-188 Angstrom wavelength observations of 108 Taurus-Perseus-Auriga region stars. The resulting data revealed the presence of far-ultraviolet emission from these regions in the 110-160 Angstrom band. The observed far-ultraviolet emission is consistent with the presence of hydrogen-like helium ions, indicating the presence of young stars. The overall energy output of these regions in the 110-160 Angstrom band is comparable to the energy output of O and B stars in the Milky Way. The observed far-ultraviolet emission from these regions is consistent with the presence of young stars, which are responsible for the observed emission. The results of this survey provide new insights into the formation and evolution of young stars, and the impact of these stars on the surrounding interstellar medium.

Table extraction from PDF documents is an essential component of many document analysis systems. However, it remains a particularly difficult task due to the diverse formats tables can take, which vary across documents. Recent advancements in the field of graph neural networks have shown potential in addressing this issue, as they can effectively capture the structural and visual information within documents. In this study, we explore the application of graph neural networks to identify and extract tables from PDF documents through a novel approach. We utilize a graph representation of the document to guide the neural network in determining table boundaries, and then apply the network to extract the actual table content. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on the PDF4ML dataset and outperforms existing table extraction techniques.

This paper explores the dynamics of incomplete information games and the impact of limited knowledge on decision-making. By modeling real-world scenarios such as the "Guess the Average" and "Beauty Contest" games, where agents' choices are influenced by incomplete information, we can better understand how different levels of reasoning affect outcomes. Our analysis of these games reveals that when agents are uncertain about each other's knowledge, they may follow complex hierarchies of reasoning, where their level of cognition can be correlated with the accuracy of their decisions. Furthermore, we show that when agents' knowledge is unlimited, these hierarchies break down, leading to more predictable outcomes. Our findings have significant implications for real-world applications, including understanding how limited knowledge affects decision-making in various fields.

In recent years, there has been a growing need for timely and accurate population data to support policy decisions and planning. The traditional approach of relying on censuses and supplementary surveys has limitations, especially in terms of cost and accuracy. This study explores the potential of using remote sensing data to estimate population data in real-time, without the need for recent census data. The proposed model combines night-time light data, historical census information, and climate data to create accurate population estimates. The model's accuracy is validated using population data from the United States, India, Mozambique, and the United Nations. The results show that the model can provide reliable population estimates, even in areas with no recent census data. The model's accuracy is further validated by comparing the model's predictions to population data from Mozambique's Demographic and Health Survey. The study concludes that the proposed model has significant potential to support policy decisions and planning in areas with limited resources and data.

Approximate membership question (AMQ) is a less precise version of basic membership question, prioritizing efficiency over precision. In AMQ, the outcome of checking if an element belongs to a set is uncertain, even when the element does not belong to the set, as long as the element does belong to the set, the outcome is always positive. In this article, we explore data structures for efficient AMQ that produce results without errors for elements not in the set, and we propose a new data structure called FPF-S set, which combines two Bloom filters to eliminate the possibility of incorrect results. The FPF-S set also has the advantage of being able to recover the first Bloom filter when the element belongs to the set, which results in a lower data usage compared to existing data structures for efficient AMQ that produce results without errors for elements not in the set.

Our research examines how to convert Feshbach-bound diatomic molecules into spin-polarized atoms using a laser pulse. This method has the advantage of not requiring a second laser, allowing for the creation of unstable polarized diatomic molecules. Instead, we utilize an in situ photoassociation technique to induce three-body recombination and transfer the molecules into spin-polarized atoms. This process is demonstrated using a $^{40}$K gas, and our results show that it is possible to create highly unstable spin-polarized potassium atoms at room temperature. This method has the potential to be applied to other atomic species, and its efficiency can be optimized by adjusting the photoassociation detuning and magnetic field.

A novel computational framework combines the strengths of the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method and the grid-based methods to simulate complex multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. This approach leverages the multi-resolution capabilities of SPH, allowing for the use of finer and coarser particle resolutions in different simulation domains. By employing this strategy, the method significantly reduces the computational resources required, particularly the memory usage and the number of particles used to model each phase. This setup enables the accurate simulation of RANS equations for a primary flow and the Lagrangian Eulerian coupling for a secondary flow with a high number of particles. This approach is successfully demonstrated in simulations of a falling wire cage and the dispersion of a seed cloud.

A new quantum machine learning framework is developed, combining quantum unsupervised and supervised learning approaches that can be executed on near-term quantum devices with limited qubits and circuit depth. This development addresses the limitations of current quantum hardware, thereby making it suitable for the near-term quantum machine learning era. By utilizing a hybrid algorithm, the unsupervised learning aspect demonstrates significant speedup in clustering tasks compared to classical counterparts, achieving a 100 times improvement in runtime. Similarly, the supervised learning method shows promising results, achieving a 92 percent test accuracy in a binary classification problem within 42 qubit gates, surpassing the minimum quantum advantage threshold. This study demonstrates the potential of quantum machine learning algorithms to achieve a 1 order of magnitude improvement in performance, thereby paving the way for substantial gains in data processing efficiency.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch has shown great potential for pitch controllability, but it has limitations in handling extreme pitch values. In this research, we introduce a new augmentation technique that utilizes sine waves to augment training data and improve the control of pitch values. Our approach leverages a simple filter to introduce variability in pitch values derived from existing sentences in FastPitch. Additionally, we develop an algorithm to fine-tune the filter for each dataset, and test the effectiveness of our technique using two datasets, TIMIT and LibriSpeech. Results demonstrate that this simple method significantly enhances FastPitch's performance, with an average F1 score improvement of 10.8% on TIMIT and 12.3% on LibriSpeech.

The widespread adoption of smart devices has led to the widespread use of the Internet of Things (IoT), resulting in numerous data streams being generated across various spatial and temporal dimensions. The analysis of IoT data on graph structures, particularly on nodes and edges, has become a pressing concern, prompting the development of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) as a potential solution. However, GNNs struggle to effectively model complex and irregular connections and are often inadequate in capturing the nuanced patterns inherent in complex linkages. To address these limitations, we propose Hopper, a cutting-edge model that seamlessly integrates the strengths of the attention mechanism from the Transformer architecture and the expressive power of GNNs, enabling the effective reasoning across multi-hop graphs. Empirical evaluations on real-world IoT data demonstrate the exceptional performance of Hopper, surpassing state-of-the-art methods, including the Transformer and GNN models, in both link prediction and spatial-temporal reasoning tasks.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production alongside a $b\bar{b}$ pair at
$\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV using 29.3 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the ATLAS detector.
We utilized the $W\rightarrow e\nu$ and $W\rightarrow \mu\nu$ decays in conjunction
with a $b\bar{b}$ pair to derive the differential cross sections for various final
state observables. These results are presented in the context of next-to-leading
order QCD predictions based on the NNPDF3.1$_{\text{zq}}$0111$^{ZV}$ PDF set.
A comparison with NNPDF3.1$_\text{Zq}$0111 $and other NLO QCD predictions reveals
excellent agreement with data across various observables. Furthermore, we
calculated the $W$ boson mass from the measured charged-lepton transverse momentum
and lepton-plus-$b$-jet transverse momentum distributions, yielding a value of
$80.02\pm 0.62$ GeV, in line with the current world average.

This study investigates user experience quality (QoE) for telepresence robot control, focusing on driving performance and user stress levels. Two experiments were conducted to assess the influence of two human-driven robots on user experience quality. Firstly, it examined the impact of robot control modes on driving performance, user stress, and satisfaction. Two modes were tested: a traditional joystick control and a more intuitive feature-based control. Secondly, it assessed the impact of two different robot designs on driving performance, user stress, and satisfaction. Two robots were tested: a humanoid robot and a wheeled robot. The results revealed that the control mode had a significant effect on user experience quality, with the feature-based control yielding better results. Additionally, the results showed that the robot design had a significant effect on user experience quality, with the wheeled robot yielding better results. The findings of this study contribute to the development of more user-friendly telepresence robots.

This study provides an accessible overview of Bayesian hierarchical linear regression models, allowing readers to derive the posterior distribution by conjugate analysis. We also calculate the predictive distribution for new data using normal and inverse-Wishford priors, then apply the concept of minimum mean square error prediction to estimate parameters. By exploring the asymptotic behavior of predictive distributions, the study confirms that as data grows, the posterior distribution converges to a singular normal distribution centered on the mean estimate, as expected. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that hierarchical models yield consistent estimates, with variance approaching zero as data grows.

The game of Mafia, also known as Murder, has gained significant popularity in party settings over the last few decades. A 2006 research paper by Hughes and Van Driel attempted to analyze the game's mechanics, but their model fell short of accurately representing the full game experience. This study aims to address this gap by developing a more comprehensive mathematical model that incorporates the specific rules of the British TV adaptation featuring Chris Tarrant.
